rv.q: The show holds up well, and director Alex Timbers (“Andrew Jackson”) nicely choreographs the rapid succession of wacky routines and guests — “Someone’s coming!”

Paul Reubens' gloriously goofy man-child returns in fine fettle, surrounded by the colorful denizens of his wonderfully warped world in a show that's both a nostalgic throwback and a welcome reminder of inspired silliness.

Mr. Reubens's Broadway debut is, among other things, a comeback attempt, two widely publicized run-ins with the law having forced him into involuntary semiretirement. With $3 million in the box-office till to date, it looks like a success. I'm fine with that: Mr.
But the Pee-wee faithful are unlikely to quibble about narrative substance while they’re busy mainlining trippy color, subversive comedy, mad energy and beloved catchphrases.
Pee-wee may be playing it safe, but perhaps he's playing it smart too.
If you never got Pee-wee's appeal, this show won't help.
For this appreciative but not adoring outsider, the show has an awful lot of bad-smell jokes and, after a while, a wearying delight in its own ingenuous ingenuity.
Newcomers are unlikely to be converted, and might just as well stay home.
It is highly original Pop-derived kitsch, executed with relish and just enough showbiz polish to keep us engaged for the equivalent length of three episodes of Pee-wee’s Playhouse.
After twenty minutes of non-characters wandering in a non-plot, speaking non-dialogue, driven by a comedian who is distinguished by his artificial non-personality, a sense of doom sets in.
What he's really cooking up, though, is a knowing Proustian reflection on time passing and innocence lost both Reubens' and our own.
Seemingly unchanged in 30 years, Reubens' Pee-wee is as dangerously uncontrollable as ever, representing the fun-loving yet wild little kid in all of us.
Acting giddy, impatient, childish and full of personality, Pee-wee Herman is simply irreplaceable.
Paul Reubens' ageless man-child is as sweetly subversive as ever in this charmingly silly Broadway revival that should delight fans both old and new.
The plot, such as it is, hinges on the possible wiring of The Playhouse for Pee-wee's computer, which turns out to be a very bad idea indeed.

From its Pledge of Allegiance opening to a typically moonstruck ending, 'The Pee-Wee Herman Show' is certain to blast 20-and-30-somethings back to their youth for their very first taste of nostalgia, complete with a 'Penny' cartoon in the middle.
Perhaps the perfect choice to guide the madness and innuendo supplied by Reubens and co-writers is Alex Timbers.
In fact, their gleeful response may be the highlight of the recycled evening of goofy shenanigans.
